theme: Engineering conventions of a SaaS product
facts: The backend services are written in Go and built as single static binaries.
The web frontend is written in TypeScript with React and Vite.

Schema changes go through goose migration files reviewed by Priya, and nothing is run by hand on production. Each migration must include a down script and be tested on staging first. Large table changes run only in the low-traffic window from 2 to 4 a.m. UTC.
Hot read queries are cached in Redis for ten minutes by default.
Full-text search is handled by OpenSearch, and we never use LIKE queries for search.
Deployments run on Kubernetes, and every release goes to a canary first.

Production releases ship on Tuesdays and Thursdays between 10 and 12 UTC, and never on Fridays. A canary receives five percent of traffic for thirty minutes before the full rollout. Hotfixes can skip the window with Priya's approval and a written incident note. If the error rate rises above 0.1 percent during rollout, the release rolls back automatically.
Branches are short-lived, named after the ticket ID with a feat/ prefix.

Every pull request needs two approvals, and the author cannot merge their own change. Changes to billing or auth need an approval from Priya in addition to the usual reviewers. Reviewers should respond within one business day, and stale pull requests get a reminder bot message. Small docs-only changes can merge with one approval.
Unit test coverage must stay at or above 80 percent for every service.
The QA lead is Sam Ortiz, who owns the end-to-end test suite.
Logs are structured JSON and include a trace ID on every line.

Errors are reported to Sentry, and any error that fires more than fifty times in an hour opens an incident ticket. Logs must never contain customer email addresses or card numbers, so use the redaction helper. Engineers may raise the log level to DEBUG while investigating, but must reset it within one hour. Error messages returned to clients use the stable error codes listed in the API docs.
Public endpoints are REST with JSON, while internal calls use gRPC.
Priya leads engineering and sets technical direction, working in UTC+1.
Tomas is the SRE on-call coordinator and works US Pacific hours.
Dana leads the frontend team and reviews all design system changes.

On-call rotates weekly, and the primary has fifteen minutes to acknowledge a page before it escalates to the secondary. Handoffs happen on Monday mornings with a written summary of open issues. Pages that wake someone up must be logged in the on-call tracker. Anyone who is on call for a whole week gets a day off the following Monday.
API docs are generated from the OpenAPI spec and published at /docs.

Secrets are stored in a managed vault, and no credentials may be committed to the repository, even in test files. Each service gets its own scoped token, rotated every ninety days. If a secret leaks, the on-call engineer rotates it within one hour and posts in the security channel. Local development uses a sample env file that contains only dummy values.
Dependency updates are batched monthly, and Dependabot opens the pull requests.

Rate limits are set at three hundred requests per minute per API key, and clients must back off exponentially on 429 responses. Rate limit rules live in the gateway config, and changing them needs two approvals. Before a big launch, the team raises the limits a week early and tells Tomas. Internal service accounts are exempt, but they still emit metrics.
The health check endpoint is /healthz and is used by Kubernetes probes.

Every new service needs a design doc reviewed by Priya and Tomas before a repo is created. The doc covers API sketches, data models, and failure handling. New engineers may not push to main during their first week, and they submit changes to a feature branch for their mentor. Design docs are archived in the engineering wiki after approval.
